tldr: ARPO enables effective end-to-end policy optimization for GUI agents using GRPO with an experience replay buffer, significantly improving in-domain task success rates in sparse-reward desktop environments.
contributions: An end-to-end policy optimization approach for training GUI agents in multi-turn, multi-modal environments using GRPO
A task selection strategy that filters for valuable tasks capable of producing successful rollouts under baseline agents
An experience replay buffer that retains successful trajectories to enhance sample efficiency and stabilize training in sparse-reward settings
Demonstration that RL substantially improves in-domain performance while offering only moderate generalization to out-of-domain tasks
methods: The authors build a vision-language GUI agent on the UI-Tars-1.5 (7B) base model with up to 15 images and 64K context length to process full GUI trajectories. They employ a distributed rollout system with 256 parallel virtual environments on OSWorld, using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) for end-to-end policy optimization with a binary trajectory reward and action format penalty. A task selection strategy curates 128 valuable tasks from OSWorld, and an experience replay buffer stores successful per-task trajectories to inject into GRPO groups when all sampled rollouts fail.
results: ARPO achieves a 29.9% success rate on standard OSWorld and 23.8% on OSWorld Hard, improving over the UI-Tars-1.5 base model by 6.4% and 5.6% respectively. In-domain success rises from 68.8% (GRPO) to 81.25% (ARPO), a 12.5% absolute improvement. Out-of-domain performance sees modest gains: ARPO scores 56.3% versus 55.2% for the base model. The replay buffer achieves a higher average trajectory reward of 0.75 vs 0.65 without it. ARPO outperforms offline preference methods, scoring 27.3% vs 26.0% (GRPO), 24.6% (KTO), 22.4% (DPO), and 21.8% (reject sampling).
limitations: RL training delivers strong gains on in-domain tasks but only moderate generalization improvements on out-of-domain tasks. Successful rollouts are rare in sparse-reward GUI environments. Training requires significant compute with 256 parallel environments. Strong generalization still depends on broader task diversity and larger-scale training compute.
